entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Wahtye, a high-ranking priest and purification priest (wab-priest) of the royal necropolis, served during the reign of King Neferirkare Kakai (c. 2446–2436 BCE), the third pharaoh of the Fifth Dynasty of ancient Egypt. His significance, largely posthumous, stems from the extraordinary discovery of his virtually intact tomb in November 2018 at Saqqara, an archaeological find that offered an unparalleled window into the daily life, religious beliefs, and artistic sophistication of Old Kingdom Egypt. Unlike many high officials whose tombs were plundered, Wahtye's burial chamber, sealed for millennia, preserved intricate wall reliefs, painted statues, and the mummy of the priest himself, providing a rich, direct source for understanding an elite individual's existence in the mid-third millennium BCE.

The tomb, an exquisitely decorated mastaba, revealed Wahtye's extensive titles, including "royal inspector," "supervisor of the royal estate," and "sole companion," underscoring his prominent position within the pharaonic administration and religious hierarchy. Its vibrant frescoes depict scenes of daily life, from boat building and pottery making to hunting and musical performances, alongside detailed funerary rituals and offerings. These reliefs are not merely decorative; they function as a "biography in stone," illustrating the idealized existence Wahtye hoped to enjoy in the afterlife and providing invaluable ethnographic data on ancient Egyptian society, economy, and culture during a period of centralized power and monumental construction.
